title: Compare and Contrast TCP and UDP Ports, Protocols, and Their Purposes

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Networks run many services at the same time. Ports help a system determine which network service should receive particular traffic.
For this objective, recognize common port numbers, the protocols associated with them, what those protocols do, and the difference between TCP and UDP.
sections.callout: Do not stop at Port 22 = SSH. Recognize secure remote command-line connection → SSH → port 22.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When CompTIA describes what a network service is doing, can you identify the protocol, its port number, and whether TCP or UDP behavior best fits the communication?
sections.callout: SERVICE PURPOSE → PROTOCOL → PORT.

sections.title: Ports and Protocols
paragraphs: An IP address identifies a device. A port helps identify a service on that device. One server can provide several services from the same IP address because each service can listen on a different port.
sections.callout: IP = which system? Port = which service?

sections.title: FTP - Ports 20 and 21
paragraphs: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) transfers files between systems. Port 21 carries the control connection, while port 20 is traditionally associated with data transfer in active FTP.
FTP does not provide the secure encrypted remote administration associated with SSH.
sections.callout: Traditional file transfer service → FTP → 20/21.

sections.title: SSH vs. Telnet

entries.title: SSH - Port 22
paragraphs: Secure Shell (SSH) provides encrypted remote command-line access for managing another system.

entries.title: Telnet - Port 23
paragraphs: Telnet provides legacy text-based remote terminal access without the encryption expected from SSH.

sections.callout: 22 secure; 23 legacy and insecure.

sections.title: SMTP - Port 25
paragraphs: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) sends and transfers email. It is not the protocol used to retrieve messages from a mailbox.
sections.callout: Send or transfer email → SMTP → 25.

sections.title: DNS - Port 53
paragraphs: Domain Name System (DNS) resolves names to IP addresses and supplies other DNS information. If a resource works by IP address but not by hostname, investigate DNS.
DNS can use both TCP and UDP. Basic queries commonly use UDP; TCP is used when reliable connection-oriented communication or larger exchanges are required.
sections.callout: Names ↔ addresses → DNS → 53.

sections.title: DHCP - Ports 67 and 68
paragraphs: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically supplies network settings such as an IP address, subnet information, default gateway, and DNS server information.
sections.callout: Automatic IP configuration → DHCP → server 67, client 68.

sections.title: HTTP vs. HTTPS

entries.title: HTTP - Port 80
paragraphs: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) carries standard web communication without HTTPS encryption.

entries.title: HTTPS - Port 443
paragraphs: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) provides encrypted web communication.

sections.callout: 80 = web; 443 = secure web.

sections.title: POP3 vs. IMAP

entries.title: POP3 - Port 110
paragraphs: Post Office Protocol 3 (POP3) retrieves email and traditionally emphasizes downloading messages from the mail server to the client.

entries.title: IMAP - Port 143
paragraphs: Internet Mail Access Protocol (IMAP) accesses and manages mailbox information on the server, supporting the same mailbox across multiple devices.

sections.callout: SMTP sends; POP3 pulls; IMAP keeps the server mailbox in sync.

sections.title: NetBIOS and NetBT - Ports 137-139
paragraphs: Network Basic Input/Output System (NetBIOS) provides legacy local-network communication and resource-related services. NetBIOS over TCP/IP (NetBT) carries those services over TCP/IP.
Ports 137 through 139 historically support name, datagram, and session functions.
sections.callout: Legacy Windows-style local networking → NetBIOS/NetBT → 137-139.

sections.title: LDAP - Port 389
paragraphs: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) accesses and works with directory information about users, groups, systems, and other organizational resources.
sections.callout: Query or access directory information → LDAP → 389.

sections.title: SMB and CIFS - Port 445
paragraphs: Server Message Block (SMB) is commonly used for network file and printer sharing. Common Internet File System (CIFS) is associated with the SMB family of file-sharing technologies.
sections.callout: Windows-style shared folders and printers → SMB/CIFS → 445.

sections.title: NetBIOS vs. SMB
paragraphs: These technologies can appear together in Windows networking, but their port recognition must remain distinct.

sections.title: RDP - Port 3389
paragraphs: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) provides graphical remote access to another computer, allowing interaction with a remote desktop rather than only a command-line shell.
sections.callout: Remote graphical Windows desktop → RDP → 3389.

sections.title: SSH vs. RDP
sections.callout: SSH = terminal; RDP = desktop.

sections.title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
paragraphs: TCP is connection-oriented. It establishes a logical connection before normal application data is exchanged and provides sequencing, acknowledgments, retransmission, and ordered delivery.
Those reliability mechanisms add overhead but help ensure that missing data is detected and resent.
sections.callout: Reliability and ordered delivery matter → TCP.

sections.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
paragraphs: TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake: SYN requests the connection, SYN-ACK acknowledges and responds, and ACK confirms the response.
sections.callout: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK indicates connection-oriented TCP communication.

sections.title: User Datagram Protocol (UDP)
paragraphs: UDP is connectionless. It sends without establishing a TCP-style connection and does not provide TCP's built-in guarantees for delivery, ordering, or retransmission.
The reduced overhead is useful when timely delivery or lower transport overhead matters more than verifying every piece of data at the transport layer.
sections.callout: Connectionless and lower overhead → UDP.

sections.title: TCP vs. UDP
sections.callout: TCP asks, Did you get it? UDP says, Sending it! The correct choice depends on the application's needs.

sections.title: TCP and UDP Protocol Recognition
sections.callout: Reliable connection-oriented delivery → TCP. Connectionless lower-overhead delivery → UDP.

sections.title: Objective 2.1 Exam Trap
paragraphs: This objective groups similar services. Identify the service first, then recall the protocol and port. If the question compares transport behavior, decide whether it wants reliability and a connection or lower overhead and connectionless delivery.

entries.title: SSH vs. Telnet
paragraphs: Both provide a remote command line. Secure and encrypted means SSH 22; legacy and unsecured means Telnet 23.

entries.title: HTTP vs. HTTPS
paragraphs: Standard web traffic uses HTTP 80; encrypted web traffic uses HTTPS 443.

entries.title: SMTP vs. POP3 vs. IMAP
paragraphs: SMTP 25 sends, POP3 110 retrieves or downloads, and IMAP 143 maintains a server-based mailbox.

entries.title: DNS vs. DHCP
paragraphs: DNS 53 resolves names. DHCP 67/68 provides automatic network configuration.

entries.title: SSH vs. RDP
paragraphs: SSH 22 supplies a secure command line; RDP 3389 supplies a graphical desktop.

entries.title: TCP vs. UDP
paragraphs: Do not reduce the comparison to slow versus fast. Ask whether the application requires connection establishment, acknowledgments, ordering, and retransmission.

sections.callout: SERVICE → PROTOCOL → PORT; then evaluate TCP versus UDP behavior when asked.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: SMB/CIFS 445 → network file and printer sharing
